note: Every fact is restated from an official State of New Jersey source fetched on the retrieved date (curl, UA 'site-reforge/1.0 (+fact check)'). 'quote' is copied verbatim from the page text; ' ... ' separates non-adjacent passages of the same source, in page order. Where two official texts disagree, both facts are kept and linked by 'conflict'. The statute text (P.L.2021, c.16 on pub.njleg.gov / pub.njleg.state.nj.us) could not be fetched (connection timeout), so no fact cites the statute directly. Plain restatement only; not legal advice.

sources.title: General Information - Legal Cannabis in New Jersey

facts.statement: New Jersey's CREAMM Act allows the legal sale and use of cannabis and cannabis products for residents 21 years and older.
facts.quote: New Jersey’s Cannabis Regulatory, Enforcement Assistance, and Marketplace Modernization (CREAMM) Act allows for the legal sale and use of cannabis and cannabis products for residents 21 years and older.

facts.statement: Adults 21 and older can buy recreational cannabis at a licensed dispensary.
facts.quote: Yes. Adults 21 years and older can buy recreational cannabis at a licensed dispensary.

facts.statement: Buying cannabis anywhere other than a New Jersey licensed dispensary is illegal, and the safety of that product cannot be guaranteed.
facts.quote: Purchasing cannabis from anywhere other than these locations is illegal and the safety of the purchased product cannot be guaranteed.

facts.statement: Legal product categories include dried flower, concentrated oils, resin, vape formulas, tinctures, topicals, syringes, lozenges, soft chews and shelf-stable food products, though availability varies by dispensary.
facts.quote: Legally allowable product categories include dried flower, concentrated oils, resin, vape formulas, tinctures, topicals, syringes, lozenges, soft chews, and shelf-stable food products but availability will vary by dispensary.

facts.statement: Federal law, the Controlled Substances Act, still prohibits the cultivation, distribution and possession of marijuana regardless of state law.
facts.quote: The Controlled Substances Act, 21 U.S.C. §§ 801 et seq., prohibits the cultivation, distribution, and possession of marijuana, for any reason, regardless of state law.

facts.statement: Each municipality sets its own regulations and zoning for the number, type and operations of cannabis businesses within its borders.
facts.quote: Municipalities determine their own regulations and zoning ordinances governing the number, type, and operations of cannabis businesses within their borders.

facts.statement: Anyone 21 or older, whether a New Jersey resident or a visitor, can buy cannabis.
facts.quote: Who can buy? Anyone - New Jersey residents or visitors - 21 years and older.

facts.statement: Dispensary staff must see a government-issued ID to confirm you are 21 or older, and they may not copy your ID or keep a record of your purchase beyond what that single transaction requires.
facts.quote: Dispensary personnel will need to see a government-issued identification card to ensure purchasers are 21 years or older. They are not allowed to make copies of your ID or retain record of your purchase beyond what is required for the completion of that single financial transaction.

facts.statement: Under the state rules, a retailer checks photo ID before letting a customer in and again before each sale, and may not keep a copy of the ID.
facts.quote: (a) Before allowing entrance to a cannabis retailer, and additionally prior to selling or serving cannabis items to a consumer, for each transaction, cannabis retailer personnel shall examine any one of the following pieces of photographic identification and shall confirm the consumer is of legal age to purchase cannabis: ... 3. The cannabis retailer shall not keep a copy of the consumer’s photographic identification.

facts.statement: A person under 21 may not purchase, acquire, accept or consume cannabis, or try to.
facts.quote: (f) Pursuant to N.J.S.A. 2C:35-10.d, a person under 21 years of age shall not purchase, acquire, accept, or consume a cannabis item, or attempt to do so.

facts.statement: A person under 21 may not enter a cannabis business unless accompanied and supervised by a parent or legal guardian, or otherwise permitted by law.
facts.quote: 1. A person under 21 years of age shall not enter, or attempt to enter, a cannabis business premises, unless accompanied by and supervised by a parent or legal guardian or otherwise permitted by law.

facts.statement: Adults who give cannabis to someone under 21, or help them buy it in any way, are subject to penalties.
facts.quote: Adults who give cannabis to individuals under the legal age, or help them buy in any way, are also subject to these penalties.

facts.statement: New Jersey state law allows adults 21 and older to have up to 6 ounces of cannabis and cannabis products in their possession.
facts.quote: New Jersey state law allows adults 21 years and older to have up to 6 oz of cannabis and cannabis products in their possession.

facts.statement: New Jersey state law allows adults 21 and older to have up to 6 ounces of cannabis and cannabis products in their possession.
facts.quote: How much cannabis am I allowed to have on me? New Jersey state law allows adults 21 years and older to have up to 6 oz of cannabis and cannabis products in their possession.

facts.statement: The state rules say it is not unlawful for a consumer to possess, purchase, transport or give away without payment up to 1 ounce of usable cannabis, or the equivalent in cannabis products, obtained directly from a licensed retailer.
facts.quote: (b) It is not unlawful, pursuant to N.J.S.A. 2C:35-10.a for: 1. A consumer to possess, display, purchase, transport, or transfer without remuneration for non-promotional, nonbusiness purposes, where the cannabis item is obtained directly from a licensed cannabis retailer: i. Up to one ounce of usable cannabis; or ... ii. Up to the equivalent of one ounce of usable cannabis as a cannabis product in solid, liquid, or concentrate form;

facts.statement: You may give up to 1 ounce (28.35 grams) of cannabis to another adult 21 or older, but you may not accept any payment or compensation for it.
facts.quote: Yes. You may give up to 28.35 grams (1 ounce) of cannabis to another adult 21 years or older. You may not accept any form of payment or compensation for the gifted cannabis.

facts.statement: In each transaction, a dispensary may sell you up to the equivalent of 1 ounce (28.35 grams) of usable cannabis.
facts.quote: In each transaction, dispensaries are allowed to sell up to the equivalent of 28.35 grams or 1 ounce of usable cannabis.

facts.statement: In one transaction you can buy up to 28.35 grams (1 ounce) of dried flower.
facts.quote: That means up to: 28.35 grams (1 ounce) of dried flower, or

facts.statement: In one transaction you can buy up to 4 grams of solid cannabis concentrate or resin, or the equivalent of 4 grams of concentrate in liquid form.
facts.quote: 4 grams of solid cannabis concentrates or resin, or the equivalant of 4 grams of concentrate in liquid form (solution in milliliters), or

facts.statement: In one transaction you can buy up to 4 grams of vaporized formulations (oil).
facts.quote: 4 grams of vaporized formulations (oil), or

facts.statement: In one transaction you can buy up to 1,000 mg of ingestible cannabis products such as gummies, for example ten 100 mg packages.
facts.quote: 1000 mg of multiple ingestible cannabis-infused products (10 100 mg packages) like gummies

facts.statement: You can combine products in one purchase, for example 14.17 grams (1/2 ounce) of dried flower and 2 grams of concentrate, or 5 packages of gummies and 14.17 grams (1/2 ounce) of dried flower.
facts.quote: A purchase of a combination of products may be 14.17 grams (1/2 ounce) of dried flower and 2 grams of concentrate, or 5 packages of gummies and 14.17 grams (1/2 ounce) of dried flower.

facts.statement: Under the state rules, a retailer may not sell more than 28.35 grams (one ounce) of usable cannabis to a consumer in a single transaction.
facts.quote: (d) The cannabis retailer shall not sell to a consumer in a single sales transaction: 1. More than 28.35 grams (one ounce) of usable cannabis;

facts.statement: The rules also cap a single sale at four grams of solid concentrate or four mL of liquid concentrate (oil), and at vaporized formulations containing no more than four mL of oil.
facts.quote: 2. More than four grams of solid cannabis concentrate or four mL of liquid cannabis concentrate (oil); 3. Vaporized formulation containing more than four mL of liquid cannabis concentrate (oil);

facts.statement: The rules cap a single sale of ingestible products at an aggregate total of 1,000 mg of THC.
facts.quote: 4. Multiple ingestible cannabis-infused products containing an aggregate total of more than 1,000 mg of THC; or

facts.statement: A combination purchase may not exceed 28.35 grams (one ounce) or the equivalent, and retailers must make a good-faith effort to stop customers from going over one ounce across multiple transactions.
facts.quote: 5. More than 28.35 grams (one ounce), or the equivalent, of some combination of usable cannabis and cannabis products. (e) The cannabis retailer shall make a good faith effort to prevent a consumer from exceeding one ounce of usable cannabis or the equivalent weight in cannabis products, in multiple sales transactions.

facts.statement: You may smoke cannabis in private spaces, but landlords may prohibit cannabis use on their property.
facts.quote: You may smoke in private spaces, however landlords may prohibit cannabis use on their property.

facts.statement: Cannabis smoking is allowed where cigarette smoking is permitted, unless stated otherwise.
facts.quote: Cannabis smoking is allowed where cigarette smoking is permitted, unless stated otherwise.

facts.statement: Generally, adults 21 and older can use cannabis on private property, but property owners can limit its use on their property.
facts.quote: Generally, an adult 21 years of age or older can use cannabis on private property. However, property owners can limit the use of cannabis on their property.

facts.statement: New Jersey's Smoke Free Air Act prohibits smoking of any kind in most public spaces, and private property owners have the right to prohibit cannabis smoking on their property.
facts.quote: New Jersey's Smoke Free Air Act prohibits smoking of any kind in most public spaces. Additionally, private property owners have the right to prohibit cannabis smoking on their property.

facts.statement: The state rules do not permit smoking, vaping or aerosolizing cannabis anywhere a federal, state or local law prohibits smoking tobacco.
facts.quote: (e) Nothing in this chapter is intended to permit the smoking, vaping, or aerosolizing of cannabis items in any place in which a Federal, State, or local law prohibits the smoking of tobacco.

facts.statement: The rules do not permit anyone to possess or use cannabis in a school, hospital, detention facility or correctional facility.
facts.quote: (d) Nothing in this chapter is intended to permit any person to possess, consume, use, display, transfer, distribute, sell, transport, grow, or manufacture cannabis or cannabis items in ... a school, hospital, detention facility, adult correctional facility, or youth correctional facility.

facts.statement: Landlords may prohibit or otherwise regulate the use, possession or transport of cannabis on their property.
facts.quote: (c) Nothing in this chapter shall prohibit a landlord from prohibiting, or otherwise regulating the consumption, use, display, transfer, distribution, sale, or transportation of cannabis items on or in that property, or portion thereof.

facts.statement: General cannabis use cannot be a determining factor in hiring or firing, but employers have the right to keep a drug- and alcohol-free workplace.
facts.quote: While general cannabis use cannot be a determining factor for hiring or firing someone, employers do have the right to maintain a drug and alcohol-free work environment.

facts.statement: In-house or contracted Drug Recognition Experts may perform random drug tests for intoxication at work, and may test anyone who appears impaired on the job or has been in a workplace accident.
facts.quote: In-house or contracted Drug Recognition Experts may perform random drug tests for intoxication at work, and may test anyone who appears to be impaired on the job, or who has been in a workplace accident.

facts.statement: You can also consume legal cannabis at licensed dispensaries with consumption areas, which admit only patrons 21 or older with photo ID.
facts.quote: You can also consume legal cannabis at licensed dispensaries with consumption areas. ... Every patron must be at least 21 years of age with photo identification to enter a consumption area.

facts.statement: Consumption areas cannot sell food or drinks; patrons may bring or order in food and drinks, but no alcohol, and no tobacco products are allowed inside.
facts.quote: No. Consumption areas cannot sell food or beverages of any kind. Patrons may bring or order in food and drinks, but no alcohol. ... No. Patrons may not bring in or consume tobacco products of any kind while inside a consumption area.

facts.statement: Medical patients must be allowed to bring their medicinal cannabis into consumption areas, but dispensaries can prohibit recreational users from bringing their own.
facts.quote: Patients must be allowed to take their medicinal cannabis into consumption areas. However, dispensaries can prohibit recreational users from bringing in their own cannabis.

facts.statement: Like open-container laws for alcohol, you may not leave a consumption area with an open package of cannabis.
facts.quote: Similar to open container laws for alcohol, patrons are not allowed to leave a consumption area with open packages of cannabis.

facts.statement: The Medicinal Cannabis Program tells patients not to smoke on federal lands or in federal buildings, or in a private vehicle in motion.
facts.quote: Do not smoke on federal lands, or in federal buildings. Do not smoke in a private vehicle in motion.

facts.statement: Growing cannabis at home is not legal; current New Jersey law does not let the Commission authorize any growing outside a business with a cultivation license.
facts.quote: Can I legally grow cannabis at home? No. Current New Jersey law does not give authority to NJ-CRC to authorize private, residential, or any growing of cannabis outside of a business with a cultivation license.

facts.statement: Medical patients and caregivers are not permitted to grow cannabis or possess a cannabis plant.
facts.quote: The law does not currently permit home grow. Patients and caregivers are not permitted to grow cannabis or be in possession of a cannabis plant.

facts.statement: Driving under the influence of cannabis is illegal in New Jersey, even though cannabis itself is legal for adults 21 and older.
facts.quote: In New Jersey, driving under the influence of cannabis is illegal, even though cannabis itself is legal for adults 21 and older.

facts.statement: This applies whether cannabis is used for recreational or medical purposes, and an impaired driver can be charged with driving under the influence (DUI).
facts.quote: This applies regardless of whether cannabis is used for recreational or medical purposes. If a driver is impaired while operating a vehicle, they can be charged with driving under the influence (DUI).

facts.statement: Cannabis DUIs are prosecuted under the same statute as alcohol DUIs, N.J.S.A. 39:4-50.
facts.quote: Cannabis DUIs are prosecuted under the same statute as alcohol DUIs: N.J.S.A. 39:4-50.

facts.statement: Police may use trained Drug Recognition Experts and other evidence to decide whether a driver is impaired by drugs.
facts.quote: Law enforcement officers may use trained Drug Recognition Experts (DREs) and other evidence to determine whether a driver is impaired by drugs.

facts.statement: For a first offense, the Commission lists a license loss of 7 months to 1 year, a $300 to $500 fine plus fees and insurance surcharges, up to 30 days in jail, and 12 to 48 hours of the Intoxicated Driver Resource Center program.
facts.quote: First Offense License loss 7 months – 1 year Monetary consequences: $300–$500 fine $230 Intoxicated Driver Resource Center (IDRC) fee $100 Drunk Driving Fund fee $100 Alcohol Education and Rehabilitation Fund (AERF) fee $75 Safe Neighborhood Services Fund fee $1,000 insurance surcharge per year for three years Additional consequences: Up to 30 days in jail 12–48 hours of the IDRC program

facts.statement: Medical patients must not operate a car, aircraft, train, stationary heavy equipment or boat while under the influence of medicinal cannabis.
facts.quote: Do not operate an automobile, aircraft, railroad train, stationary heavy equipment or a vessel while under the influence of medicinal cannabis.

facts.statement: Nothing in the state cannabis rules allows driving under the influence of, or while impaired by, cannabis.
facts.quote: (a) Nothing in this chapter is intended to allow driving under the influence of cannabis items or driving while impaired by cannabis items or to supersede laws related to driving under the influence of marijuana or cannabis items or driving while impaired by marijuana or cannabis items.

facts.statement: You cannot take cannabis bought in New Jersey home to another state; transporting cannabis across state lines is still illegal.
facts.quote: Can I take my purchase back home to another state? No. It is still illegal to transport cannabis across statelines.

facts.statement: Medical patients must not transport medicinal cannabis across state lines.
facts.quote: Do not transport medicinal cannabis across state lines.

facts.statement: The program advises patients to keep medicinal cannabis in its original labeled packaging, keep it at home, and transport it only when absolutely necessary.
facts.quote: Medicinal cannabis should be kept in its original labeled packaging. ... Keep medicinal cannabis at home and only transport it when absolutely necessary.

facts.statement: New Jersey's Medicinal Cannabis Program (previously the Medicinal Marijuana Program) helps registered patients under the care of licensed healthcare practitioners access cannabis-based medicine from regulated and monitored facilities.
facts.quote: New Jersey’s Medicinal Cannabis Program (previously the Medicinal Marijuana Program) helps registered patients under the care of licensed healthcare practitioners safely access cannabis-based medicine from regulated and monitored facilities.

facts.statement: The program exists under the New Jersey Compassionate Use Medical Marijuana Act (CUMMA) and the Jake Honig Compassionate Use Medical Cannabis Act.
facts.quote: The current Medicinal Cannabis Program (MCP) is made possible through the enactment of New Jersey Compassionate Use Medical Marijuana Act (CUMMA) and the Jake Honig Compassionate Use Medical Cannabis Act.

facts.statement: Medicinal cannabis treatment is not covered by any health plan in New Jersey.
facts.quote: Is medical cannabis covered by health insurance or Medicaid? No. Medicinal cannabis treatment is not covered by any health plan in New Jersey.

facts.statement: The program does not share a patient's enrollment information without the patient's written consent.
facts.quote: We take patient privacy seriously and do not share enrollment information without patients’ expressed consent in writing.

facts.statement: The program's Patient Services Unit can be reached at (609) 292-0424 or Medcannabis@crc.nj.gov.
facts.quote: Patient Services Unit Phone: (609) 292-0424 Fax: (609) 292-9432 Email: Medcannabis@crc.nj.gov

facts.statement: To register as a patient you must have a bona fide relationship with a healthcare provider registered with the program, be a New Jersey resident, and be diagnosed with a qualifying medical condition by a registered New Jersey healthcare practitioner.
facts.quote: To become a registered patient with the New Jersey Medicinal Cannabis Program (NJMCP), you must: Maintain a bona fide relationship with a healthcare provider who is registered with the program. ... Be a New Jersey resident. Be diagnosed with a qualifying medical condition by a New Jersey healthcare practitioner registered with the New Jersey Medicinal Cannabis Program.

facts.statement: A bona fide relationship means the practitioner has treated you for at least one year, or has seen you for the condition on at least four visits, or has taken over care of the condition after a comprehensive medical history and physical examination, including a review of your records from other treating physicians.
facts.quote: The practitioner-patient relationship has existed for at least one year; or The healthcare provider has seen and/or assessed the patient for the debilitating medical condition on at least four visits; or The healthcare provider assumes responsibility for providing management and care of the patient’s qualifying medical condition after conducting a comprehensive medical history and physical examination, including a personal review of the patient’s medical record maintained by other treating physicians

facts.statement: Approved qualifying conditions include amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, anxiety, cancer, chronic pain, dysmenorrhea, glaucoma, inflammatory bowel disease (including Crohn's disease), intractable skeletal muscular spasticity, migraine, multiple sclerosis, muscular dystrophy, opioid use disorder, HIV/AIDS, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), seizure disorder (including epilepsy), sickle cell anemia, terminal illness with a prognosis of less than 12 months to live, and Tourette syndrome.
facts.quote: Approved qualifying medical conditions include: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis Anxiety Cancer Chronic pain Dysmenorrhea Glaucoma Inflammatory bowel disease, including Crohn’s disease Intractable skeletal muscular spasticity Migraine Multiple sclerosis Muscular dystrophy Opioid Use Disorder Positive status for Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) and Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS) Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) Seizure disorder, including epilepsy Sickle cell anemia Terminal illness with prognosis of less than 12 months to live Tourette Syndrome

facts.statement: The program's patient FAQ lists the same approved conditions but does not include sickle cell anemia.
facts.quote: The approved medical conditions include: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis Anxiety Cancer Chronic pain Dysmenorrhea Glaucoma Inflammatory bowel disease, including Crohn’s disease Intractable skeletal muscular spasticity Migraine Multiple sclerosis Muscular dystrophy Opioid Use Disorder Positive status for Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) and Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS) Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) Seizure disorder, including epilepsy Terminal illness with prognosis of less than 12 months to live Tourette Syndrome

facts.statement: Opioid use disorder qualifies as a standalone condition, either to treat the disorder itself or for chronic, painful withdrawal symptoms.
facts.quote: Opioid use disorder qualifies as a standalone debilitating medical condition for the program. Opioid use disorder patients may be eligible for medical cannabis to treat the opioid disorder itself, or if they suffer from chronic, painful withdrawal symptoms.

facts.statement: Adults and minors with a qualifying medical condition may participate in the Medicinal Cannabis Program.
facts.quote: Adults and minors with a qualifying medical condition may participate in the Medicinal Cannabis Program.

facts.statement: Patients registered in another state's program may get a nonrenewable, six-month New Jersey card for their stay, after consulting a registered New Jersey healthcare practitioner who enrolls them.
facts.quote: Medicinal cannabis patients from other states may register for a nonrenewable, six-month MCP card for use during their stay in New Jersey. Out-of-state patients will need to consult with a registered New Jersey healthcare practitioner who will enroll them in our registry.

facts.statement: Step one is to find out whether your current healthcare provider participates in the program, or to find a participating practitioner.
facts.quote: Determine if your current healthcare provider is a participant in the program or find a participating healthcare practitioner.

facts.statement: If you and your provider think cannabis will help, the provider gives you an Authorizing Healthcare Practitioner Statement with a reference ID number and a registry ID number, which you need to open your patient portal account and register.
facts.quote: If you and your health care provider think you will benefit from adding cannabis to your course of treatment, they must provide you with an Authorizing Healthcare Practitioner Statement. The statement will include a reference ID number and a registry ID number, which you will need to establish an account in the patient portal and complete a registration process.

facts.statement: You then create a username and password for an account in the program's patient portal.
facts.quote: You will need to create a username and password to set up an account in the Medicinal Cannabis Program patient portal.

facts.statement: Once the account is active, you complete registration by choosing an Alternative Treatment Center (dispensary) to buy from, which you can change at any time, uploading proof of New Jersey residency, choosing your ID card option, and uploading a recent photo.
facts.quote: Once your account is activated, you will complete the registration process, by: Identifying an Alternative Treatment Center where you will be able to purchase your medicinal cannabis doses. (You will be able to change your ATC in the portal at any time.) Uploading proof of your New Jersey residency ... Selecting your ID card option. ... Uploading a recent full-face, front facing photograph

facts.statement: Proof of residency is a current New Jersey government-issued ID, or, without one showing your physical address, two other proofs such as a utility or cell phone bill from the last 90 days, the last three monthly bank statements, the last three consecutive pay stubs, or an official deed.
facts.quote: A current New Jersey government-issued ID or two proofs of residency If you do not have a current New Jersey state issued ID reflecting your physical address you may provide two other proofs of residency from the list below: a utility or cell phone bill from the last 90 days ... last three monthly bank statements showing the patient’s name and address last three consecutive pay stubs an official deed

facts.statement: The photo must be a recent full-face, front-facing photograph taken within the last 60 days against a plain white background, without a hat, glasses or filters, with eyes open and a neutral expression.
facts.quote: A recent full-face, front facing photograph taken within the last 60 days taken against a plain, white background taken without a hat, or glasses taken with eyes open and facial expression neutral taken without filters

facts.statement: The patient FAQ says a renewal photo must be one recent passport-size color photo against a white background, with nothing obscuring your features, taken no more than 30 days before you submit.
facts.quote: A person applying for issuance or renewal of registration as a qualifying patient shall provide one recent passport-size color photo, taken against a white background. No hat, glasses, or anything else that could obscure your features is allowed in the photo and it must have been taken no more than 30 days before you submit for renewal.

facts.statement: If a minor's authorizing provider is not a pediatrician, the parent or guardian also needs a Minor Attestation from a pediatrician.
facts.quote: (If the authorizing provider is not a pediatrician, parents/guardians of minor patients will also need to acquire a Minor Attestation from a pediatrician affirming their belief that the minor is likely to receive therapeutic or palliative benefit from the medical application of cannabis.)

facts.statement: The registration page says the parent or guardian of a minor patient must request a Minor Attestation from the authorizing provider if that provider is not a pediatrician.
facts.quote: (Parents/guardians of minor patients will also need to request a Minor Attestation from from the authorizing provider if the provider is not a pediatrician.)

facts.statement: Registration is online only, and patient services representatives can walk you through setting up or accessing your account.
facts.quote: Participation in the Medicinal Cannabis Program requires online registration. Our patient services representatives are happy to walk you through the process if you need assistance setting up or accessing your account.

facts.statement: Most registrations cannot be expedited; the exception is only for patients with terminal cancer or another terminal illness with a prognosis of less than 12 months to live.
facts.quote: Most registrations cannot be expedited. Exception to the regular registration process is reserved only for patients diagnosed with terminal cancer or who are otherwise terminally ill with a prognosis of less than 12 months to live as indicated in their recommendation by their health care provider.

facts.statement: Once you have created your portal account and started registration, you may buy at a medical dispensary with your government-issued ID while your registration is under review; renewing patients are not eligible for this.
facts.quote: Yes. First you must create a user account and log into your portal to initiate registration. Once you have initiated registration, you may visit a medical dispensary with your government issued ID. The medical dispensary will be able to look up your information in the Medicinal Cannabis Program registry. Patients that are renewing are not eligible.

facts.statement: Renewal reminders are sent 60 days before your ID expires, and you may renew at any time after that.
facts.quote: Renewal reminders are sent 60 days before the current ID expires. Patients and caregivers may renew at any time after that.

facts.statement: Digital ID cards are free for new and renewing patients and caregivers; a physical ID card costs $10.
facts.quote: The Medicinal Cannabis Program now offers free digital ID cards for new and renewing patients and caregivers. ... New and renewing patients and caregivers can also request a physical ID card for a $10 charge.

facts.statement: Both digital and physical ID cards are valid for two years.
facts.quote: $10 if you would like to receive a physical ID card. Digital ID cards are free. Both kinds of ID cards are valid for two years.

facts.statement: Registered patients whose condition makes them physically unable to go to a dispensary (ATC) may have up to two caregivers, who may buy medicinal cannabis without the patient present.
facts.quote: Patients registered in the Medicinal Cannabis Program may elect to have up to two caregivers if their condition renders them physically unable to go to an alternative treatment center (ATC). Designated caregivers may purchase medicinal cannabis from an ATC without the patient present.

facts.statement: Caregivers, typically a friend or family member chosen by the patient, can be added during or after registration and must get a program ID card through the same registration process as patients.
facts.quote: Caregivers are chosen by the authorized patient – typically a friend or family member – and can be added at any time during registration, or after. Caregivers must acquire a Medical Cannabis Program identification card through the same registration process as patients.

facts.statement: A caregiver must be a New Jersey resident and at least 18 years old.
facts.quote: Do I Qualify? Be a New Jersey resident Be at least 18 years old

facts.statement: Caregivers who are not immediate family members must submit fingerprints for a criminal background check.
facts.quote: Caregivers who are not immediate family members are required to submit fingerprints for a criminal background investigation.

facts.statement: A caregiver added after the patient has received an ID gets the same expiration date as the patient, which may be less than two years away.
facts.quote: Note: If a patient adds a caregiver after they have received their ID, the caregiver's ID will have the same expiration date as the patient which may be within less than two years.

facts.statement: Someone who only drives you to the dispensary and does not assist you inside does not need to register as a caregiver.
facts.quote: Someone driving you to the ATC, but not assisting you inside does not need to register as a caregiver with the NJ-CRC.

facts.statement: Patients receive cannabis orders from their doctor or other healthcare practitioner of up to 85 grams for every 30-day period, filled at state-licensed Alternative Treatment Centers or dispensaries.
facts.quote: As part of medicinal treatment, patients receive cannabis orders from their doctor or other healthcare practitioner of up to 85 grams for every 30-day period. Cannabis orders are filled at one of the state-licensed Alternative Treatment Centers (ATCs) or dispensaries across New Jersey.

facts.statement: The most a patient or designated caregiver may buy is 85 grams (3 oz) for a 30-day period, the practitioner sets the dosage, and terminally ill patients are exempt from the maximum.
facts.quote: The maximum amount of medical cannabis that a qualifying patient or the patient’s designated caregiver is allowed by law to purchase is 85 grams (3 oz) for a 30-day period; however, your authorizing health care practitioner will determine your dosage. Terminally ill patients are exempted from the maximum limits.

facts.statement: The same patient FAQ gives the maximum monthly allowance, taken as flower, as 84 grams, or 3 ounces.
facts.quote: If the recommendation is for the maximum monthly allowance and I want it to be in flower, how much would that be? That would be 84 grams, or 3 ounces.

facts.statement: Patients may buy any combination of flower, concentrates, oil and ingestibles as long as they stay within their recommendation's monthly limit.
facts.quote: Yes, so long as you stay within the limit of your recommendation’s limit per month, you can purchase any combination of flower, concentrates, oil and/or ingestibles.

facts.statement: Patients may buy up to 85 grams (3 oz) every 30 days, while recreational consumers may buy only 28.35 grams (1 oz) in a single transaction.
facts.quote: Patients may purchase up to 85 grams (3 oz) at a time every 30 days, while recreational consumers are only allowed to purchase 28.35 grams (1 oz) in a single transaction.

facts.statement: A patient or caregiver must show their program (MCP) ID to buy products on a dispensary's medical menu.
facts.quote: Yes. A patient or caregiver must present their MCP ID to the dispensary to purchase cannabis products available on the medical menu.

facts.statement: The state sales tax on medicinal cannabis is 0%, though municipal taxes vary up to 2%.
facts.quote: The state sales tax on medicinal cannabis is 0%. Municipal taxes vary up to 2%.

facts.statement: Medicinal cannabis is prioritized over recreational supply, and dispensaries that sell medicinal cannabis must give patients priority service.
facts.quote: Medicinal cannabis is prioritized over cannabis for recreational use, so there is always a supply for patients. ... Dispensaries that sell medicinal cannabis are also required to provide priority service to patients.

facts.statement: A visiting patient's six-month card allows purchases without state sales tax and use of patient-only lines and patient-only hours at dispensaries.
facts.quote: Visiting patients can get a nonrenewable, six-month MCP card that will allow them to make purchases without state sales tax on cannabis and cannabis products, use patient-only lines, and purchase during patient-only hours at dispensaries.
